refutation.quote: T 1.0 (seeds of T1, unpaired totals): 390 (100 zeroed) and 372 (1,000) against 410, 0 loops in all.
refutation.note: The cued base at T 1.0 / top-p 1.0 on MATH-500 is in scope. The 3-token opening is prefilled and identical in every arm. Zeroing 1,000 'loop' neurons gives 0 loops but drops the score from 410 to 372, so computation after the opening moves accuracy by 38 problems. The theory says 'nothing after the opening adds' and predicted 407 [392, 422] for this held-out cell (t70). That was its largest held-out loss, -1.39 nats. The scope excludes weight-difference models, not neuron ablations, so this item is not excluded. It is a single unpaired sample, and an ablation could cause general damage, so on its own it is moderate evidence. The stronger in-scope contradiction is the rival's turn-2 duel test k5, run on the theory's own T3 file. Among plain answers that do not self-open, the ones that later say 'Wait'/'Hmm' score +0.356 above the ones that do not. The defended interval was [-0.15, 0.10]. Also read: result-fc8f8b (WSP-2 edit 397/500, consistent with the theory), result-882fa7 (Wait steering adds nothing to the cued base, consistent), result-dc15a1, result-296647 (the only after.jsonl item matching 'on its own'; it is about self-distillation and not relevant).

wins_judgement: Offline total +0.72. p1 (D = 0.00, gain +0.63): the theory centred tighter at -0.02 while both nulls said -0.05 with wider intervals. A reader of Wang et al. App C.8 (uncued answers opening with a paragraph break score 71.6 % vs 77.9 % cued; +47 points within a problem) would have predicted much the same, so the mechanism added only interval width. p2 (R = 1.21, gain +0.44): the theory said 1.0 and the nulls 0.9. The length match follows from the whole-mode claim, but the measured value sits near the top of the interval. p3 (AUROC 0.54, gain -0.34): the per-problem propensity the theory needed barely clears its own refutation line of 0.53, which points to per-sample noise. Held-out: t52 (edited base 85/100 vs 74 predicted, +0.85) and t53 (random edit 38, +0.61) come from 'an edit that makes the base write the opening gives cued accuracy'. That is a real mechanism-earned gain, though anyone who knew the cue's effect would lean the same way. t67/t64/t66 (cued arms near 410-430) are what the nulls also said. t70 (-1.39) is a loss the mechanism caused, because it says later computation cannot matter.
rival:
Duel state: loses to rival (total -8.844). Turn 1: all three tests had the same prediction from both sides. k3 (+0.21 at T 0.6) is outside the theory's scope anyway. Turn 2 separates the two on three tests, each -3.0 for the theory. k4: no self-open but Wait/Hmm later, minus cued on the same problems, measured -0.075; theory [-0.60, -0.33], rival [-0.30, 0.02]. k5: within non-self-opened plain answers, marker minus no marker, measured +0.356; theory [-0.15, 0.10], rival [0.07, 0.41]. k6: hard328 analogue, measured -0.10; theory [-0.47, -0.19], rival -0.10. I read rivals/r5-m10.turn2/p5.py. It implements the recipe as written: first row per problem_index kept, grader v3 rescored, self-open as '
Okay' in text[:60], case-sensitive 'Wait'/'Hmm' anywhere, mean M minus mean N; n_L = 67 for k4. One caveat weakens the rival's reading but not the theory's loss. The 60-character rule labels only 94 of 500 T3 answers self-opened, while the board counts 168 'Okay' openings. The example row in L opens with '

Okay' after about 190 characters of prompt continuation. So part of the 'late self-check' group is a late 'Okay' opening, not a mid-answer switch. Either way the answers' accuracy is not fixed in 'the first few tokens' as the theory states. The theory's opening-only account explains the turn-1 numbers but not the turn-2 numbers. The rival explains both.

novelty.nearest: Wang et al., Base Models Can Reason By Taking a Cue From Training Data, App C.8 and Table 12: uncued Olmo-3-7B responses that begin with a paragraph break (95 % then continue with 'Okay') have pass@1 71.6 % vs 24.8 % for single-newline openings, 41.5 % overall, against 77.9 % with the forced '.\n\n Okay' cue; within a problem the paragraph-break openings are 47 points more often correct.
novelty.difference: The theory adds a T 1.0 / top-p 1.0 same-problem comparison (self-opened accuracy equals cued accuracy, D = 0, at matched length), the decomposition of the +38.6-point cue gain as (1 - self-open share) x accuracy gap, and the claim that nothing after the opening adds. The paper reports the observational mixture at T 0.6 only, and the last of these claims failed the duel.

import_carries_gain.which: The only import is 2509.06608 (an RL steering vector acts as a first-token substitution; prefixing 'To' gives about 75 % of its gain). It supplies the framing, but no winning number is computed from it. p1, p2, t52 and t53 rest on the board's own cue numbers. The paper that would carry p1, Wang et al. App C.8, is not imported. The theory cites it only through knowledge-8a31ad for the 42.2 -> 77.9 gain.

verdict: refuted: duel state 'loses to rival' (-8.84 nats). In scope, on its own T3 file, plain answers that do not self-open but self-check later score +0.36 above other plain answers and come within 0.075 of cued answers on the same problems, which contradicts 'nothing after the opening adds'. Result-460e0a's 410 -> 372 drop under a fixed cue points the same way, and the part that survives (self-opened answers score like cued ones) is largely in Wang et al. App C.8.
